disease: Spastic ataxia 8, autosomal recessive, with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy

messages.content: You are a clinical geneticist. You are given evidence about one rare disease and a cohort of patients described by HPO terms. Exactly one patient has the disease. Use only that evidence as your knowledge of the disease. Be explicit about which findings in the report drove each placement, and about findings that argue against it.

REPORT ON Spastic ataxia 8, autosomal recessive, with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy (NKX6-2, OMIM:617560): # Clinical Identification and Phenotypic Profile of Spastic Ataxia 8 (SPAX8 / NKX6-2) ## 1. Executive Summary & Diagnostic Approach to SPAX8 Spastic ataxia 8, autosomal recessive, with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy (SPAX8; OMIM #617560) is an ultrarare neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic loss-of-function or missense variants in the homeobox transcription factor gene *NKX6-2* (Chelban et al., 2017, PMID: 28575651; Dorboz et al., 2017, DOI: 10.1093/brain/awx207) [F1, F3]. Clinically, SPAX8 manifests along a continuous severity spectrum anchored by progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity pyramidal spasticity, nystagmus, and dysarthria (Chelban et al., 2017, DOI: 10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.05.009; Chelban et al., 2018, GeneReviews NBK531509) [F2, F6, F13]. A critical diagnostic pitfall is the presumption that diffuse central nervous system (CNS) hypomyelination is an obligate finding. Neuroimaging evaluations demonstrate that biallelic *NKX6-2* mutations can present as childhood-onset spastic ataxia with isolated cerebellar atrophy in the complete absence of overt cerebral leukodystrophy (Chelban et al., 2017, PMID: 28575651; Chelban et al., 2020, DOI: 10.1111/ene.14082) [F2, F11]. Clinicians must therefore identify SPAX8 based on a constellation of core motor and oculomotor features, distinct pertinent negatives, and inheritance patterns rather than relying strictly on the presence of hypomyelination on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). --- ## 2. Clinical Phenotypic Spectrum and Observed Frequencies per Cohort To pick an individual affected by SPAX8 out of a group of patients presenting with overlapping complex neurodevelopmental or spastic ataxia syndromes, phenotypic manifestations must be quantified using exact cohort denominators. The following table compiles systematically reported phenotypes across established clinical cohorts, listing original paper phrasing, standardized Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, exact numerators and denominators, and resolvable source identifiers. ### Table 1: Systematically Reported Phenotypes in SPAX8 Cohorts | Phenotypic Finding (Paper Wording) | Standardized HPO Term | Cohort Frequency (n/N) | Cohort Description & Study Citation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Lower limb spasticity / Spastic paraparesis** | Spasticity (HP:0001257) | **7/7** (100%) | Discovery cohort across 3 families (Chelban et al., 2017, PMID: 28575651) [F1, F13, F15] | | **Cerebellar ataxia** | Cerebellar ataxia (HP:0001251) | **7/7** (100%) | Discovery cohort across 3 families (Chelban et al., 2017, DOI: 10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.05.009) [F1, F13, F15] | | **Nystagmus** | Nystagmus (HP:0000639) | **2/2** (100%) | Sibling cohort with homozygous missense variant (Bereshneh et al., 2020, PMID: 32004679) [F6, F9] | | **Nystagmus** | Nystagmus (HP:0000639) | Core finding across **25/25** reviewed cases | Aggregated review of 13 families (Chelban et al., 2018, GeneReviews NBK531509; Anazi et al., 2017, DOI: 10.1007/s00439-017-1843-2) [F8] | --- ## 3. Discriminating Features from Phenotypic Mimics When evaluating a patient with early-onset spasticity, cerebellar signs, and white matter abnormalities, SPAX8 must be differentiated from three primary clinicoradiological mimics: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD / *PLP1*), Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease 1 (PMLD1 / *GJC2*), and *POLR3*-related leukodystrophies (4H leukodystrophy). ### Table 2: Differential Diagnosis Matrix and Discriminating Validity | Differential Condition | Key Clinical Mimicry | Discriminating Distinctions Favoring SPAX8 (*NKX6-2*) | Distinguishing Confidence Level | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Pelizaeus-Merzbacher Disease (PMD) / *PLP1*-Related Disorders (SPG2)** | Early nystagmus, hypotonia progressing to spastic quadriparesis, diffuse central hypomyelination | • **Autosomal recessive inheritance** in SPAX8 distinguishes it from X-linked recessive inheritance of *PLP1* (Wolf et al., 2019/2025, GeneReviews NBK1182; Chelban et al., 2018) [F10, F12].
• Absence of generalized demyelinating polyneuropathy (which occurs in *PLP1* null mutations) (Wolf et al., 2025; Bereshneh et al., 2020) [F12].
• Preservation of intellectual faculties into later childhood in milder SPAX8 presentations (Chelban et al., 2017, 2018) [F8, F10]. | **High** (Mendelian inheritance pattern and neurophysiology reliably distinguish kindreds) | | **Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-Like Disease 1 (PMLD1 / *GJC2*)** | Autosomal recessive inheritance, congenital/early nystagmus, ataxia, spasticity, diffuse central hypomyelination | • **Absence of early choreoathetoid involuntary movements**: PMLD1 frequently manifests with early prominent choreoathetosis and extrapyramidal dyskinesia, which are atypical in SPAX8 (Chelban et al., 2018; Ganguly et al., 2023) [F4, F10].
• Prominent isolated cerebellar atrophy can occur in SPAX8 without overt leukodystrophy, which is atypical for *GJC2* (Chelban et al., 2017, 2020) [F2, F11]. | **Moderate** (Clinical overlap is extensive; definitive discrimination often requires targeted gene sequencing) | | ***POLR3*-Related Leukodystrophies (4H Syndrome)** | Childhood-onset cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, dysarthria, motor deterioration, hypomyelination | • **Absence of hypodontia** (HP:0000668) and abnormal dentition in SPAX8 (Chelban et al., 2018) [F10, F14].
• **Absence of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism** (HP:0000818) and delayed puberty in SPAX8 (Chelban et al., 2018) [F10, F14].
• Absence of myopia or optic atrophy hallmarks common to *POLR3* deficiency (Chelban et al., 2018; Wolf et al., 2021) [F10, F14]. | **Very High** (Systemic endocrine and dental examination conclusively resolves the differential) | | **Hereditary Axonal Motor Neuropathies / Pure HSPs** | Progressive lower limb spasticity, gait impairment, distal weakness (wrist/foot drop) | • Presence of **early cerebellar nystagmus (HP:0000639)** and **cerebellar ataxia (HP:0001251)** distinguishes SPAX8 from pure hereditary spastic paraplegias (Chelban et al., 2017; Bereshneh et al., 2020) [F4, F6, F7].
• Central hypomyelination or cerebellar vermian atrophy on brain MRI excludes pure lower motor neuron disorders [F2, F4, F7]. | **High** (Combination of oculomotor signs and neuroimaging) | --- ## 4. Pertinent Negatives and Exclusionary Findings A critical strategy for isolating SPAX8 from broad spastic ataxia panels is evaluating for systemic and neurological findings that have been systematically investigated and found absent. The presence of any of the following features argues strongly **against** a diagnosis of *NKX6-2*-related disorder (Chelban et al., 2018; Chelban et al., 2020, DOI: 10.1111/ene.14082; Wolf et al., 2021, DOI: 10.1038/s41582-020-00432-1) [F10, F14]: 1. **Hypodontia or Oligodontia (HP:0000668):** Systematically absent in SPAX8; points directly toward *POLR3A/POLR3B/POLR1C* disorders (4H syndrome) [F10, F14]. 2. **Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (HP:0000818):** Systematically absent; indicates *POLR3*-related disease [F10, F14]. 3. **Primary Demyelinating Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy:** Nerve conduction studies in SPAX8 demonstrate preserved peripheral myelin sheaths without generalized conduction slowing or uniform demyelinating profiles (Wolf et al., 2025; Buttermore et al., 2013, DOI: 10.1002/jnr.23197) [F12, F14]. Where peripheral neuropathy occurs in SPAX8, it is an atypical, late-stage, motor-predominant axonal degeneration (HP:0003477) (Bereshneh et al., 2020, PMID: 32004679) [F4, F7, F14]. 4. **Extensive White Matter Cavitation or Cystic Degeneration:** Neuroimaging in SPAX8 reveals hypomyelination (T2 hyperintensity with mild T1 hyperintensity/isointensity) or cerebellar atrophy, but lacks cavitation, rarefaction, or cystic breakdown typical of vanishing white matter disease or mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies (Sharma et al., 2025, DOI: 10.1002/jmri.29558; Chelban et al., 2020) [F4, F14]. 5. **Primary Retinal Dysplasia or Congenital Cataracts:** Retinal architecture is preserved in SPAX8, ruling out syndromes such as Marinesco-Sjögren syndrome (*SIL1*) or Cockayne syndrome [F14]. 6. **Severe Congenital Microcephaly:** Head circumference is typically normal at birth in SPAX8, distinguishing it from primary microcephalic leukodystrophies [F14]. --- ## 5. Phenotypic Stratification by Age, Sex, Variant Type, and Position ### Age of Onset Stratification SPAX8 presents across two major clinical trajectories that reflect developmental timing rather than distinct genetic etiologies (Chelban et al., 2017, DOI: 10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.03.011; Chelban et al., 2020, DOI: 10.1111/ene.14082) [F3]: - **Early Infantile / Neonatal Presentation:** Characterized by early-onset pendular or horizontal nystagmus (HP:0000639) evident within the first 6 months of life, accompanied by marked axial hypotonia (HP:0001252), failure to achieve head control (4/5 individuals in Dorboz et al., 2017), severe global psychomotor delay (HP:0001263), and rapid transition to spastic quadriparesis (HP:0001257) with pseudobulbar dysarthria and dysphagia [F3, F9]. Developmental motor regression (HP:0002376) is frequently observed in this subgroup (Baldi et al., 2018) [F9, F10]. - **Late Childhood / Juvenile Presentation:** Characterized by relatively preserved early motor milestones (e.g., achieving independent walking), followed by insidious-onset progressive cerebellar ataxia (HP:0001251), spastic paraparesis, slurred speech, and loss of ambulation during late childhood or adolescence (Chelban et al., 2017) [F2, F3]. Cognition may remain relatively spared [F8, F10]. ### Sex Distribution SPAX8 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Across all reported cohorts (Chelban et al., 2017; Baldi et al., 2018; Chelban et al., 2020; Bereshneh et al., 2020), disease penetrance and clinical severity show no statistically significant sex bias, affecting male and female siblings with equal frequency and progression rates [F1, F2, F10]. ### Variant Type and Position: Refutation of Binary Genotype-Phenotype Models Early hypotheses proposed that biallelic protein-truncating variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice-site) caused severe infantile hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, whereas missense substitutions in the conserved homeobox domain resulted in milder childhood-onset spastic ataxia with preserved ambulation. **This genotype-phenotype correlation has been definitively refuted by cohort analyses** (Baldi et al., 2018, DOI: 10.1111/cge.13221; Bereshneh et al., 2020, PMID: 32004679; Chelban et al., 2018, GeneReviews NBK531509) [F16]. Severe infantile presentations with profound developmental arrest, early motor regression, and permanent lack of ambulation have been documented in individuals harboring homozygous missense mutations within the homeodomain (e.g., p.Phe167Leu) (Baldi et al., 2018; Bereshneh et al., 2020) [F16]. Consequently, clinicians cannot predict mild versus severe disease course based solely on whether a variant is missense or truncating [F16]. --- ## 6. Literature Divergences, Contested Hypotheses, and Resolving Data Several discrepancies exist in published literature regarding cohort counts, neuroimaging obligacy, cognitive penetrance, and clinical frequencies. These issues are detailed below alongside their resolving evidence: ### 1. Foundational Discovery Cohort Size Discrepancy - *Literature Error / Contested Claim:* Multiple secondary literature sources and review articles erroneously cite the original discovery publication by Chelban et al. (2017, PMID: 28430856 / PMID: 28575651) as describing 14 affected individuals from 8 families [F13]. - *Resolving Evidence:* The foundational discovery cohort published by Chelban et al. (2017, *Am J Hum Genet*, PMID: 28575651) comprised **7 affected individuals from 3 unrelated families** [F1]. The expanded count arose from later multi-center aggregations, including Chelban et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1111/ene.14082), which identified 11 new cases from 8 new families, and the GeneReviews synthesis (Chelban et al., 2018) reviewing 25 individuals across 13 families [F1, F2, F8]. ### 2. Obligate Central Hypomyelination versus Non-Leukodystrophic Presentation - *Contested Claim:* Diffuse cerebral hypomyelination (HP:0003429) is a universal, obligate neuroimaging hallmark present in 100% of biallelic *NKX6-2* patients [F11, F13]. - *Resolving Evidence:* Diffuse hypomyelination is **not** obligate. In the discovery cohort (Chelban et al., 2017, PMID: 28575651), only Family 3 presented with diffuse brain hypomyelination; affected individuals in Families 1 and 2 (childhood-onset spastic ataxia) exhibited **isolated cerebellar atrophy (HP:0001272) without overt hypomyelination** (Chelban et al., 2017, 2020) [F2, F11, F13]. Approximately 20% to 30% of reported individuals display predominant cerebellar vermian atrophy without classic leukodystrophy [F2, F11]. Treating hypomyelination as a mandatory inclusion criterion leads to underdiagnosis of childhood-onset SPAX8. ### 3. Cognitive Impairment: Severe Intellectual Disability versus Cognitive Preservation - *Contested Claim:* Intellectual disability is universally moderate-to-severe across all SPAX8 patients [F8, F10]. - *Resolving Evidence:* This divergence stems directly from **ascertainment bias**. Kindreds identified through intellectual disability and congenital encephalopathy sequencing pipelines (e.g., Anazi et al., 2017, DOI: 10.1007/s00439-017-1843-2; Lan et al., 2025) report profound cognitive deficiency and developmental arrest [F8]. Conversely, cohorts ascertained through adult or pediatric movement disorder and spastic ataxia clinics (Chelban et al., 2017, 2018) describe patients with preserved intellectual faculties and normal speech comprehension despite severe motor disability [F8, F10]. Cognitive impairment is therefore variable and correlates with early-onset developmental disruption rather than representing an obligate primary feature across all ages. ### 4. Epileptic Seizures and Leukodystrophic Dissociation - *Contested Claim:* Epilepsy (HP:0001250) selectively tracks with severe diffuse cerebral hypomyelination [F15]. - *Resolving Evidence:* Chelban et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1111/ene.14082) demonstrated that epilepsy dissociates from neuroimaging severity: seizures can occur in individuals lacking overt hypomyelination, while patients with extensive diffuse hypomyelination may remain completely seizure-free [F5, F15]. Seizures occurred in 2 of 6 families evaluated by Baldi et al. (2018), confirming that epilepsy is an unpredictable secondary feature (33%) rather than an obligate manifestation of white matter pathology [F9]. ### 5. Developmental Regression Prevalence - *Contested Claim:* Developmental regression (HP:0002376) is rare, occurring in fewer than 15–20% of patients [F9]. - *Resolving Evidence:* Baldi et al. (2018, DOI: 10.1111/cge.13221) documented developmental and motor regression in **3 of 6 families (50%)**, and Bereshneh et al. (2020) observed motor regression in 2 of 2 affected siblings, demonstrating that regression is an under-recognized hallmark in early-onset SPAX8 rather than an exceptional outlier [F9]. ### 6. Occurrence of Peripheral Axonal Neuropathy - *Contested Claim:* Peripheral nervous system involvement is entirely absent in SPAX8 [F14]. - *Resolving Evidence:* Bereshneh et al. (2020, PMID: 32004679) and Almatrafi et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1002/jgm.3196) reported affected siblings with homozygous *NKX6-2* mutations who developed motor-predominant **peripheral axonal neuropathy (HP:0003477) with wrist drop and foot drop** (2 of 4 individuals assessed) [F4, F7, F14]. While electrophysiology confirms preserved peripheral myelin sheaths (excluding primary demyelinating polyneuropathy), secondary distal axonal degeneration represents a genuine, low-frequency (<10%) manifestation of SPAX8 [F4, F7, F12]. --- ## 7. Cross-Cutting Patterns and Clinical Synthesis Integrating the clinical, radiological, and genetic data reveals several cross-cutting pathophysiological principles that inform diagnostic practice: 1. **Dissociation Between Cardinal Syndromic Hallmarks and Neuroimaging Penetrance:** Diffuse hypomyelination, while eponymous, is non-obligate. The homeobox factor NKX6-2 plays distinct temporal roles in forebrain oligodendroglial myelination versus cerebellar circuit maintenance. In older-onset patients, cerebellar degeneration may proceed in the absence of overt forebrain dysmyelination (Chelban et al., 2017, 2020) [F2, F11]. Clinicians evaluating spastic ataxia panels lacking leukodystrophy must keep *NKX6-2* on their differential for isolated cerebellar atrophy [F2]. 2. **Decoupling of Oculomotor and Paroxysmal Manifestations from Structural White Matter:** Nystagmus is present in virtually all SPAX8 patients regardless of whether white matter is intact or severely hypomyelinated (Chelban et al., 2018) [F6]. Similarly, seizure susceptibility occurs independently of leukodystrophy severity (Chelban et al., 2020) [F5]. This suggests *NKX6-2* functions in inhibitory interneuron circuit development and cerebellar-vestibular integration independently of its structural role in myelin maintenance. 3. **Failure of Binary Truncating/Missense Predictions in Homeodomain Proteins:** Classic genotype-phenotype paradigms (truncating = null/severe; missense = hypomorphic/mild) fail in SPAX8 (Baldi et al., 2018; Bereshneh et al., 2020) [F16]. Specific homeodomain missense substitutions (such as p.Phe167Leu) likely exert dominant-negative, chromatin-trapping, or structural destabilizing effects that equal or exceed the pathogenic impact of complete genetic nulls [F16]. 4. **Secondary Axonopathy Mimicry:** The appearance of wrist drop and foot drop in rare kindreds reflects length-dependent axonal degeneration secondary to axo-glial signaling disruption rather than a primary peripheral demyelinating polyneuropathy (Bereshneh et al., 2020; Buttermore et al., 2013) [F4, F7, F12]. ### Actionable Diagnostic Algorithm for the Clinician To pick an affected individual with SPAX8 out of an undifferentiated cohort of complex neurodevelopmental and spastic ataxia patients: 1. **Screen for Core Triad:** Identify patients exhibiting the invariant combination of **cerebellar ataxia (HP:0001251)**, **pyramidal lower-limb spasticity (HP:0001257)**, and **nystagmus (HP:0000639)** (Chelban et al., 2017; Bereshneh et al., 2020) [F6, F13, F15]. 2. **Verify Autosomal Recessive Inheritance:** Confirm absence of X-linked pedigree transmission, distinguishing SPAX8 from *PLP1*-related PMD [F10, F12]. 3. **Rule Out Pertinent Negatives:** Confirm the **absence of hypodontia** (HP:0000668) and **hypogonadotropic hypogonadism** (HP:0000818) (ruling out *POLR3* leukodystrophy), the absence of primary choreoathetosis (favoring SPAX8 over *GJC2*), and the absence of primary demyelinating polyneuropathy on nerve conduction studies [F7, F10, F12, F14]. 4. **Evaluate Neuroimaging Broadly:** Review brain MRI for either **diffuse cerebral hypomyelination** OR **isolated/predominant cerebellar atrophy**; do not exclude *NKX6-2* if cerebral white matter myelination appears normal (Chelban et al., 2017, 2020) [F2, F11]. 5. **Genetic Confirmation:** Perform targeted sequencing or whole-exome sequencing for biallelic variants in *NKX6-2*, interpreting both truncating and homeobox missense variants as capable of causing full-spectrum, early-onset disease [F16]. ## Sources 1. ranking.for: This is the strongest match because he has the report’s core triad: ataxia, spasticity with hyperreflexia, and nystagmus, plus hypotonia, motor delay, and loss of ambulation, all compatible with an early/severe progressive SPAX8 course.
ranking.against: No brain MRI result is provided to show either hypomyelination or cerebellar atrophy; however, the report explicitly states that hypomyelination is non-obligate. Recorded absence of seizures does not argue materially against SPAX8 because seizures are variable.

ranking.for: She has the core motor-ocular pattern of nystagmus, ataxia, appendicular spasticity/tetraparesis, hypotonia, severe developmental impairment, loss of walking, and delayed CNS myelination, consistent with severe infantile NKX6-2 disease.
ranking.against: Optic atrophy is specifically described in the report as atypical for SPAX8 and more suggestive of a POLR3-related mimic; recorded absence of cerebellar atrophy also removes one supportive imaging feature, although it is not required.

ranking.for: Lower-limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, ataxia, axial hypotonia, cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, severe developmental delay/intellectual disability, and contractures fit the reported SPAX8 spectrum, especially an early-onset severe form.
ranking.against: Nystagmus—the report’s near-universal/core oculomotor feature—is not recorded, and developmental regression is explicitly absent despite being a common feature of severe early-onset cases. No hypomyelination is reported, though its absence would not exclude SPAX8.

ranking.for: Nystagmus, lower-limb spasticity, Babinski sign/hyperreflexia, axial hypotonia, developmental regression, severe global delay, profound intellectual disability, inability to walk, seizures, and cerebellar vermis abnormality are compatible with the severe end of the reported NKX6-2 spectrum.

ranking.for: Lower-limb spasticity, cerebellar atrophy, developmental delay/intellectual disability, and seizures overlap with reported SPAX8 manifestations; peripheral neuropathy can rarely occur in SPAX8, although reported cases were motor-predominant axonal neuropathy.
ranking.against: Nystagmus and gait ataxia are explicitly absent, despite nystagmus being a core finding and ataxia being invariant in the discovery cohort. Primary microcephaly argues against SPAX8, and the observed sensory axonal neuropathy differs from the report’s unusual motor-predominant axonal neuropathy.

rounds.what_the_report_lacked: Confidence would be substantially improved by biallelic NKX6-2 variant results and segregation/inheritance data; age at onset and progression of nystagmus, ataxia, and spasticity; detailed MRI characterization for diffuse hypomyelination versus isolated cerebellar atrophy; and explicit assessment of hypodontia/oligodontia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, choreoathetosis, and nerve-conduction findings distinguishing axonal from primary demyelinating neuropathy.
